chief_complaint: inability to breastfeed and profound fatigue since childbirth
hpi_details: 32F post-severe postpartum hemorrhage 3 months ago presenting with agalactia, amenorrhea, secondary hypothyroidism, and low cortisol.
ideas: She thinks her utter exhaustion and inability to produce milk are the result of severe postpartum depression and exhaustion following her difficult delivery.
concerns: She is worried that her profound weakness will cause her to collapse while caring for her three-month-old baby alone at home.
expectations: She hopes to receive treatment to restore her physical strength so she can take care of her baby and return to work when maternity leave ends.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Sheehan Syndrome (Postpartum Hypopituitarism) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Sheehan Syndrome (Postpartum Hypopituitarism) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes assessing and replacing glucocorticoid deficiency before starting levothyroxine, since thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated central adrenal insufficiency, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Sheehan Syndrome (Postpartum Hypopituitarism).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Postpartum thyroiditis (isolated thyroid dysfunction) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of adrenal crisis (fainting, low blood pressure) — the cortisol deficiency component can be life-threatening.
management_principles: Assess all pituitary axes and replace glucocorticoid deficiency before starting levothyroxine, because thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated central adrenal insufficiency
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Sheehan Syndrome Postpartum Hypopituitarism: inability to breastfeed and profound fatigue since childbirth. 32F post-severe postpartum hemorrhage 3 months ago presenting with agalactia, amenorrhea, secondary hypothyroidism, and low cortisol.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Sheehan Syndrome Postpartum Hypopituitarism.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Sheehan Syndrome Postpartum Hypopituitarism.
reference_soap.plan: Urgently assess for adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis. Obtain pituitary-axis testing and pituitary MRI as appropriate, but give stress-dose hydrocortisone immediately if adrenal crisis is suspected. Replace glucocorticoid deficiency before initiating levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism. Arrange urgent Endocrinology follow-up for ongoing hormone replacement and reproductive counseling.

teaching.one_liner: Severe blood loss during delivery can cause the pituitary gland to infarct, leading to failure of multiple hormone axes — inability to breastfeed (no prolactin), absent periods, and low thyroid/cortisol hormones.
red_flags: Signs of adrenal crisis (fainting, low blood pressure) — the cortisol deficiency component can be life-threatening

must_ask.say: Did you have severe bleeding or need a blood transfusion during delivery?
Have you been unable to produce breast milk?
Have your periods returned since delivery?
How is your energy, and do you feel cold often?
How many months ago did you deliver?

history.answer: Ever since I gave birth three months ago, I haven't been able to produce any breast milk at all, and I feel completely exhausted all the time.
I gave birth three months ago, and these problems began right after my delivery.
The lack of milk started on the very first day in the hospital, and this extreme exhaustion has been constant and slowly worsening ever since.
My breasts never became full or tender, and not a single drop of milk or colostrum ever came in, so we had to switch completely to formula.
No, my period has not returned at all since giving birth three months ago.
It is an overwhelming, heavy fatigue where I can barely find the strength to get out of bed or care for my baby.
Yes, I had a very complicated delivery with severe bleeding right after birth and had to receive emergency blood transfusions in the ICU.
Yes, I feel freezing cold all the time, even when the room is warm and my husband feels comfortable.
I feel dizzy and lightheaded whenever I stand up too quickly, almost like I might black out.
I haven't gained weight, but my appetite has been very poor and I've actually lost about four pounds without trying.
My skin has become noticeably dry and flaky, and I've noticed I am losing hair under my arms and in my pubic area.
I feel drained and overwhelmed, but I don't feel hopeless or sad like postpartum depression; my body simply has no physical energy.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I haven't had any unusual headaches, and my vision has been completely normal with no blurry spots.
I occasionally feel mildly nauseated, but I haven't had any vomiting or stomach pain.
No, I haven't had any chest pain, heart palpitations, or shortness of breath.
Any physical effort makes the exhaustion worse, and resting helps a little but never fully recharges me.
I tried resting more, drinking herbal lactation teas, and taking a multivitamin, but none of it helped at all.
It has made it nearly impossible to care for my newborn without constant help from my husband and mother, and I haven't been able to return to work.
I felt like I was just failing as a new mother and thought the traumatic birth and postpartum depression had completely drained my milk and energy.

I'm terrified that I'm going to pass out while holding my three-month-old baby and accidentally drop or hurt her. I'm hoping you can find out what's physically draining me and give me something to get my strength back so I can care for my baby.
I have a history of high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, but no other chronic medical conditions.
Aside from my delivery three months ago where I had the massive hemorrhage and ICU admission, I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure, along with an over-the-counter multivitamin.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I used to have an occasional glass of wine on weekends, but I have not had any alcohol since becoming pregnant.
I work full-time as an accountant, though I am currently on extended maternity leave, and I live with my husband and our new baby.
My mother has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of pituitary disorders, thyroid disease, or autoimmune problems.
My last menstrual period before getting pregnant was about a year ago, and before pregnancy my cycles were regular every twenty-eight days.
We have not been sexually active since delivery, I am not using any contraception, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 98/64 mmHg, heart rate 60 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.3°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Blood pressure drops from 98/64 mmHg sitting to 86/56 mmHg on standing with pulse rising to 74 beats/min, producing mild lightheadedness.
Appears chronically exhausted, lethargic, and pale, but oriented and cooperative.
Mild conjunctival pallor bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Pupils equal and reactive to light; visual fields are full to confrontation with no bitemporal deficits.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, without nodules or goiter.
Breasts are soft and involuted without palpable masses, engorgement, tenderness, or expressible milk.
Regular rate and rhythm with mild bradycardia; normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Skin is cool, pale, and dry, with noticeable thinning of axillary hair and no cutaneous hyperpigmentation.
Symmetric deep tendon reflexes with noticeably delayed relaxation phase at the ankles; plantar responses are flexor.
